hits.text: We also measured the layer dependence of Raman spectra at room temperature from 1 layer (1L) to 7L and the bulk sample, as shown in Figure 2b. We note that most of these peaks can be observed from bulk to 5L MnPS3 samples. In 4L and 3L samples, only the P 5 and P6 can be observed. In the 2L case, only P6 can be observed, but all peaks become unobservable in the monolayer. The possible reasons are the photoinduced degradation of the monolayer sample or the light -matter interaction in monolayer sample being too weak to have a detectable Raman signal, similar to that in monolayer NiPS3. 33 The intensities of Raman peaks increase from 2L to 7L and slightly decrease in the bulk sample due to the optical interference e ff ects between the sample and SiO 2 /Si substrate, similar to the reported measurements in other layered materials. 35,36 The frequencies of intralayer Raman modes in most layered materials will show a shift as the layer number increases due to coupling between adjacent layers. 37 However, for MnPS3, we found that the frequencies of all Raman modes remain almost constant from 2L to bulk samples. This implies that the interlayer coupling of MnPS 3 is very weak compared to that of other layered materials, such as transition metal dichalcogenides. 38,39 This is consistent with other materials of the MPX3 family such as FePS3, where the antiferromagnetic transition temperature (Ne el temperature, T N) is almost independent of the layer numbers. 20 We also measured the layer dependence of Raman spectra and intensity curves of P 2 to P8 normalized by P6 at di ff erent temperatures, as shown in Figures S1 and S2.

Because the P2 mode at 155 cm -1 is associated with vibration of Mn 2+ ions, 26 measurement of temperaturedependent Raman spectra could allow us to detect the spinrelated phase transition. Figure 3a shows the Raman spectra of 130L (90 nm) MnPS3 from 4 to 300 K. Here we just examined the 130L sample because the phase transition of MnPS 3 should be weakly dependent on the layer numbers due to weak interlayer coupling. Obviously, all peaks show an expected red shift with temperature increasing due to anharmonic terms in the lattice potential energy. 40 Remarkably, the P2 peak at around 155 cm -1 gradually disappears at around 80 K, while a new peak at 151 cm -1 gradually appears below 50 K. The temperature-dependent frequencies of all peaks are presented in Figure 3b, which clearly shows the frequency changes of these peaks in the sample. The frequency hopping of the P2 peak suggests a spin-related paramagnetic -antiferromagnetic phase transition, 13 which we will discuss later. Figure 3c shows the temperature-dependent polarized Raman spectra of 130L MnPS3. The line widths of these peaks have been signi fi cantly

narrowed at low temperature, which helps us to distinguish the two components of P5 more clearly. For the P6 peak, it becomes an asymmetrical line shape including two peaks below 110 K. These polarization properties of P5 and P6 at low temperature also support that the Raman mode should belong to the C 2/ m group, as we discussed in Figure 2.

hits.text: In order to do a structural characterization of MnPS 3 , Raman spectroscopy with a laser wavelength of λ = 532 nm on different exfoliated flakes is performed at room temperature. The result is depicted in figure 4.3. On the left side, four different Raman profiles are plotted. On the right side, the corresponding locations on the sample are imaged. The green line illustrates the Raman spectrum of the substrate. The other three lines represent Raman profiles of MnPS 3 at different flake positions with different thicknesses. Via an optical microscope one can estimate the thickness t i of the spot i comparatively: t 3 > t 1 > t 2 . We see that the intensity of the Raman modes scales with the thickness of the flake, e.g. for peak P 5 and P 6 . This is in accordance with literature [58, 85]. For MnPS 3 at room temperature eight Raman modes are reported: P 1 = 114 cm -1 , P 2 = 155 cm -1 , P 3 = 227 cm -1 , P 4 = 248 cm -1 , P 5 = 274 cm -1 , P 6 = 384 cm -1 , P 7 = 570 cm -1 and P 8 = 584 cm -1 [85]. The first two peaks correspond to vibrations including the Mn 2+ ion, the other six peaks represent molecular-like vibrations originating from the (P 2 S 6 ) 4 -structure [57, 85, 87]. Peak P 2 , P 4 , P 5 , P 6 and P 8 can be seen in the Raman profiles of all positions. Peak P 3 is clearly visible in profile 1, while peak P 1 and P 7 are barely observable in the profiles 1 and 3. Since the flake at position 2 is thinner, not all peaks appear in profile 2.

hits.text: To investigate the correlation between the spin-order of MnPSe3 and Raman scattering, we measured the Raman spectra of MnPSe3 with different thicknesses as a function of temperature. Fig. 2c and d show representative Raman spectra of bulk MnPSe3 with seven characteristic peaks from 25 to 300 K. Raman modes at high frequencies (P4-P7) are related to the vibrational modes of the [P2Se6] 4clusters, while the low-frequency peaks (P1-P3) are attributed to the vibrations involving the heavy Mn atoms [34]. The intensities of P1-P3 are relatively weak compared to those of P4-P7 (Fig. S4). To illustrate the variation of peak position and intensity, we ampli fi ed the Raman spectrum in the low frequency region as shown in Fig. 2c (the same treatment for few-layer MnPSe3) and normalized the intensity variation in the following discussion. As for the P1 peak, it appears at 82.8 cm  1 , which is related to magnetic Mn ions. A previous study found that a phonon peak ~ 86 cm  1 appeared below TN and disappeared above TN [34]. For our experimental result, P1 can still be observed at room temperature (Enlarged P1 region in Fig. S5), which will be discussed later. Interestingly, it was found that the intensity of P1 is enhanced at low temperatures. We normalized and plotted the intensity as a function of temperature (Fig. 2e). The intensity of P1 fi rstly exhibits a sharp drop and then remains stable as the temperature increases from 25 K to 300 K. The critical transition temperature corresponds exactly to the N  eel temperature of ~70 K. hits.text: We note that in the spectra for thinner samples there are several peaks that originate from multi-phonon scattering at ~210, ~590, and ~800 cm -1 (see Supplementary Fig. 8). Some of these peaks are strongly enhanced due to the resonance effect. Similar enhancement effects on multiphonon peaks due to resonance have been observed in other 2D materials 36 -38 . For example, the relative intensities or the line shapes of P 3 at ~210 cm -1 or the peak at ~590 cm -1 vary with the excitation laser energy, which is a clear indication of resonant processes (see Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Fig. 9). We further checked the temperature dependence of P3 for 1 -4L NiPS3 (see Supplementary Fig. 10). Since the frequency and the intensity of P3 does not exhibit any signi fi cant change near the Néel temperature, we can safely conclude that P3 is not related to the magnetic ordering.
